content: Dog bites can result in severe and potentially life-altering consequences for children and adolescents. Teaching young individuals how to appropriately interact with dogs may play a role in reducing the incidence of dog bite injuries. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of educational programs aimed at children and adolescents in preventing dog bite injuries and mitigating their consequences. To conduct this evaluation, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group’s Specialised Register, CENTRAL, CAB Abstracts, Zetoc, SIGLE, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ERIC, PsycInfo, SPECTR, CINAHL, National Research Register, LILACs, African Healthline, Science Citation Index, Social Science Citation Index, CurrentClinicalTrials.gov, Centrewatch, Controlledtrials.com, Vetgate, and the WHO database. The search was completed on July 18, 2008. Additionally, bibliographies of relevant reviews and trials were examined, and experts in the field were contacted for further information. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomised controlled trials and controlled before-and-after studies that assessed the effectiveness of educational interventions targeting individuals under the age of 20 for the prevention of dog bites. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of studies to identify eligible trials. They also extracted data from the selected studies and reached out to the authors of these studies for additional information when necessary. Ultimately, two studies met the inclusion criteria. However, neither of these studies directly measured the primary outcome of interest, which was the rate of dog bites. Both studies were randomised controlled trials conducted in kindergarten and primary school settings, and their methodological quality was assessed as moderate. One of the studies demonstrated that children in the intervention group exhibited fewer instances of inappropriate behavior when observed in the presence of a dog following a 30-minute educational session. The other study reported an increase in knowledge and caution among participants after completing an informational program. The authors concluded that there is no direct evidence to support the notion that educational programs can reduce the rate of dog bites among children and adolescents. However, educating children under the age of 10 in school environments may improve their knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors toward dogs. The effectiveness of similar educational interventions in non-school settings remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. High-quality studies that specifically measure dog bite rates as an outcome are urgently needed. At present, the available evidence does not support the use of educational programs as a standalone public health strategy to prevent dog bite injuries and their associated consequences.
